Rental

Rental

PricesHow it worksKitsFAQ

Prices

Try it for a weekend.

Not sure a tent is for you? Take one out before you buy. Rafael Duarte looks after the rental shelf and will help you choose.

  • Tent rental, weekendFriday to Monday€38
  • Tent rental, 7 daysCollect and return on any shop day€72
  • Pack & sleep kit, weekendPack, sleeping bag and mat€29

How it works

Four steps, no deposit paperwork.

  1. 01Reserve onlineChoose dates and a tent.
  2. 02Collect Friday from 15:00We show you how to pitch it.
  3. 03Return Monday by 12:00Dry or damp, we do not mind.
  4. 04We check, dry and log itEvery night goes in the log.

What is in the kit

Everything but the food.

A tent rental includes the tent, pegs, guy lines, a repair patch and a stuff sack. The pack and sleep kit adds a 48 litre pack, a sleeping bag rated to −5 °C comfort and an insulated mat.

Everything we rent is gear we also sell, so you can buy what you liked on Monday and we will take the rental fee off the price within seven days.

FAQ

Rental questions.

Can I collect on a Saturday?
Yes. Collection is from 15:00 on Friday, or any shop day by arrangement. Opening hours are on the Visit page.
What if something tears?
Tell us on return. Normal wear is on us; a repair is charged at the bench price, for example €18 for a patch up to 10 cm.
Can I rent for longer than 7 days?
Yes, ask at the shop. Longer rentals are priced per extra day.
Do you rent in winter?
Three-season tents and kits all year, the Cairn 3 four-season by request.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
StoryPeopleHow we test

About

About Yamabiko

StoryPeopleHow we test

Our story

A shop that sold what it carried.

In 2011 Ines Calder opened a small shop at 14 Quarry Lane, Harrow Gap, after years of buying gear that looked right on the shelf and failed on the second night out. She decided to sell only what she had slept in herself.

That rule is still the one we keep. Every tent, pack and layer on the shelves has been carried, weighed and used for at least ten nights by one of the seven of us, and the numbers on the spec sheet are the ones we measured.

Fifteen years on there is a repair bench behind the counter, a rental shelf for people who want to try before they buy, and an online catalogue that tells you the weight before the price.

People

Seven people, one rule.

  • Ines CalderFounder, buying

    Opened the shop in 2011 and still signs off every product.

    Tests tents in the shoulder seasons
  • Tomas RehnWorkshop lead

    Runs the repair bench and the weigh-in scale.

    Tests zips, seams and fabric
  • Amara OkaforTents & shelter

    Pitches every tent twice before it is shelved.

    Tests tents in wind and rain
  • Lukas BrandtPack fitting

    Leads the Thursday evening pack fittings.

    Tests packs over a full weekend
  • Mei Lin HoLayers & sleep

    Chooses the warm things and sleeps in them first.

    Tests jackets and bags on cold nights
  • Rafael DuarteRentals

    Looks after the rental shelf and the return log.

    Tests the kits between rentals
  • Sofie LundOnline orders & returns

    Answers every message within one working day.

    Tests the packaging, not the gear

How we test

Three principles.

  1. Ten nights first. Nothing is shelved before it has spent ten nights outside with one of us.
  2. Measure, then write. We weigh and measure ourselves and publish those numbers, not the maker's.
  3. Mend before replace. If it can be fixed at the bench, we say so, even if that means we sell less.

posts.title: The Mensah family: three nights at Lake Orrin
posts.excerpt: Two adults, one seven-year-old and a tent meant for two.
posts.content:
Two adults, one seven-year-old and one tent that was meant to sleep two. The Mensah family took a Ridgeline 2 to Lake Orrin for three nights in early September, and they would do it again, with a bigger porch.

The route is an easy 6 km from the road to a flat, sheltered shore. Kofi carried the tent at 1.38 kg and the sleeping bags; Ama carried the food and a 48 litre Tarn pack that she adjusted twice on the way in. Their son, Nii, carried his own bear and a headtorch.

The first night was the test. The tent sleeps two, so Nii went in the middle with his feet toward the door, and nobody slept badly. The rain came on the second afternoon for about two hours, and the fly kept the inner dry, though the porch, which is small, held three pairs of boots and nothing else.

What they would change: a groundsheet for the porch, a second lantern and a longer first day. What they would keep: the short walk in, the quiet and the way the tent packs to 42 × 14 cm, small enough that it rode on the outside of the pack for the whole route. Gear used: Ridgeline 2 Tent, Tarn 48 Pack.

posts.title: Hanne Vos: nine days on the Grey Saddle route
posts.excerpt: Nine days solo with a 0.98 kg tent.
posts.content:
Hanne Vos is in her sixties and has walked the Grey Saddle route four times. This year she took nine days, on her own, with a Saddleback 1 at 0.98 kg and a rain shell that stayed in the pack until day four.

She started in dry, cool weather on the plateau and finished in a wind that took the guy lines hard on the last col. The Saddleback held. Peak height is 96 cm, so she sat up to cook but did not stand, and she says that is the trade she is happy to make for a tent that weighs less than a litre of water.

The Mistline shell, at 0.29 kg, was the item she used least and valued most. When the cloud came down on day four she wore it for six hours, and when she took it off it packed into the lid pocket of the pack.

She weighed her full pack on the first morning at 9.8 kg including food. Her advice: weigh everything, write the numbers down, and carry nothing you cannot name a use for. Gear used: Saddleback 1 Tent, Mistline Rain Shell, Scree 30 Daypack.

posts.title: Jonas & Priya: Cairn 3 in February
posts.excerpt: Minus twelve at the hut, a calm night in the tent beside it.
posts.content:
Jonas and Priya booked a hut for a February weekend, then added a Cairn 3 to the plan so they could try a night outside. It was minus twelve when they arrived and a clear, still night.

The Cairn 3 weighs 2.64 kg, the heaviest tent on our shelf, because it is a four-season tent built for snow load and wind. They shared it with a friend and packed it to 50 × 18 cm. Pitching took twelve minutes with gloves on after one practice run in the car park.

In the tent they were warm enough in Lowtide bags with a mat each. They report condensation on the inside of the fly by morning, which froze, and which they shook off from the inside before packing.

Their list of what to do differently: a longer foam mat, a second stove, and a stuff sack for the wet fly. Their verdict is that a four-season tent is a luxury for most trips and the right answer for a few. Gear used: Cairn 3 Tent, Lowtide Sleeping Bag.

posts.title: How we weigh a tent
posts.excerpt: Hanging scale, dry bag, every peg counted.
posts.content:
Every number on our spec sheets comes from the hanging scale in the workshop. Tomas Rehn weighs each tent dry, in its own bag, with all the poles, pegs and guy lines that come in the box.

We do this because maker weights are often given for the tent without pegs, or for a size we do not stock. A tent listed at 1.2 kg can arrive at 1.5 kg once you add what you need to pitch it.

We weigh three times and write down the middle figure. Then the tent is pitched, measured at its peak and packed again to record the packed size, with the stuff sack closed and not squeezed.

The result is a spec sheet where the weight is the weight you will carry. You can see the Ridgeline 2, Saddleback 1 and Cairn 3 side by side on the Compare page.

posts.title: Reproofing a rain shell in four steps
posts.excerpt: When water stops beading, wash it first.
posts.content:
When water soaks into the outer fabric of a rain shell instead of beading off, the shell has not stopped working; the surface treatment has worn. It is a ten-minute job, and our bench does it for €35 if you prefer.

First, wash the shell on a gentle cycle with a technical cleaner, not ordinary detergent. Second, rinse it twice. Third, while it is still damp, spray or wash in a reproofing treatment, following the label for the fabric. Fourth, tumble dry on low for twenty minutes, or hang it and iron on a low setting through a cloth.

Mei Lin Ho does this to our test shells every autumn, and says that a shell reproofed twice a year is a shell you stop thinking about. If the seams have started to peel, bring it to the bench: that is a different repair.

The Mistline Rain Shell weighs 0.29 kg and is a good one to practise on.

posts.title: What is in a weekend rental kit
posts.excerpt: A pack, a bag and a mat for €29.
posts.content:
The pack and sleep kit is our most-rented item at €29 for a weekend. Rafael Duarte packs each one himself and checks it against a list before Friday.

It contains a 48 litre pack, a sleeping bag with a comfort rating of −5 °C and an insulated mat. Add a tent for €38 and you have a full weekend shelter, sleep and carry for €67.

Most people who rent it are checking three things: whether they like carrying a pack, whether they sleep outside at all, and how cold they get. We ask for the answers on Monday, because they tell us what to recommend if you decide to buy.

Rentals are cleaned, dried and logged on return, and the log is how we know which items have the most nights in them. Reserve online on the Rental page.
